title: Trump Signs Order to Create First-Ever US Space Academy
summary:
In a surprise announcement on Friday, President Donald Trump signed an executive order to create the United States' first-ever Space Academy. The announcement came during a ceremony at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Texas, where Trump was honoring the four-person Artemis II crew.

Trump compared the new academy to prestigious institutions like the US Naval Academy in Annapolis, Maryland, and the US Military Academy at West Point, New York. "They're all great. But ... we're gonna have an academy for what the people in this room love the most," he said. "That's really exciting."

The order also establishes a presidential commission to advise on the academy's creation, led by NASA administrator Jared Isaacman. Other top officials include Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Air Force Secretary Troy Meink. Graduates would serve the US Space Force, NASA, and the civilian flight industry.

At the ceremony, Trump presented the Congressional Space Medal of Honor—the highest civilian honor for space achievement—to the Artemis II crew: NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, and Christina Koch, along with Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen. In April, the crew looped around the far side of the moon, taking humans farther into space than ever before. This mission is a key step in the administration's plan to return astronauts to the moon by 2028.

Trump recounted how a meeting was interrupted by news of the crew's achievements. "I was at a very important meeting with the biggest people in the country," he said. "And somebody said, 'I'd like to watch Artemis.' I said, 'You would? Really?'" He paused the meeting, and everyone watched, spellbound.

The crew also presented Trump with a gift: a blue flight jacket with the NASA logo. "Mr President, when we were in your office and you were so gracious to us—lavishing us with gifts and so much of your time—we had mentioned getting you one of these blue flight jackets," Glover said. "And so here we have your jacket today."

Space has been a major priority for Trump, who signed the law creating the Space Force in 2019. The new academy is another bold step in that direction.
why_it_matters: The creation of a Space Academy would treat space as a permanent arena for military and civilian leadership, not just a series of missions. For today's students, it could open a new pathway to careers in the Space Force, NASA, and the growing commercial space industry.

background_read: President Donald Trump (the U.S. president who signed the executive order) announced the new Space Academy at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Texas, the center that manages America's astronaut corps.
NASA (the U.S. civilian space agency) has sent astronauts to the moon before, but the Space Force—the U.S. military branch dedicated to space, created in 2019—has never had its own academy.

The U.S. Naval Academy and the U.S. Military Academy at West Point train future military officers; the new Space Academy is meant to produce officers and experts for the Space Force, NASA, and private space companies.
The Artemis II crew, made up of NASA and Canadian astronauts, recently completed a flight around the far side of the moon as part of a larger effort to return humans to the moon by 2028.

A presidential commission, led by NASA's administrator and including the defense and Air Force secretaries, will now advise on how to build the academy; many details such as its location and curriculum remain open, but the move treats space as a permanent part of American defense.

perspectives.description: Supporters will see the Space Academy as a bold investment in America's future in space, creating a pipeline of officers and engineers. It gives space exploration the same prestige as the military academies and signals that careers in civilian spaceflight matter.

Critics may worry about the cost and duplication, since NASA and the Space Force already train specialists. They may also ask whether a new academy is the best use of resources when NASA's moon timeline has big technical and budget challenges.

The article frames the academy as part of a longer pattern of building institutions when a new branch of national defense emerges. Just as past generations created academies for naval and military officers, the Space Force era is generating its own educational system.

Many key details remain open: where the academy will be located, what students will study, and how it will coordinate with NASA and private companies. The presidential commission will need to answer those questions before the first cadets arrive.
